variants.title: Count the quorum
variants.context: etcd provides one durable order of committed operations while a voting majority can communicate. Three voters need two; five need three; a two-member cluster tolerates no failure. It prefers unavailability over split-brain writes.
variants.prompt: An etcd cluster has three voting members. How many must be able to communicate for writes to progress?
variants.explanation: Two of three form a majority, so one member can fail.

mistakes.feedback: All three would leave no failure budget.
One is not a majority of three.

variants.title: Count the quorum
variants.context: etcd provides one durable order of committed operations while a voting majority can communicate. Three voters need two; five need three; a two-member cluster tolerates no failure. It prefers unavailability over split-brain writes.
variants.prompt: Five voting members. How many failures can the cluster tolerate while still accepting writes?
variants.explanation: Three must remain, so two can fail.

mistakes.feedback: With three gone only two remain, which is not a majority.

variants.title: Count the quorum
variants.context: etcd provides one durable order of committed operations while a voting majority can communicate. Three voters need two; five need three; a two-member cluster tolerates no failure. It prefers unavailability over split-brain writes.
variants.prompt: A two-member cluster. How many member failures can it tolerate?
variants.explanation: Both members are required; a two-member cluster tolerates no failure. Use an odd voter count.

mistakes.feedback: Losing one leaves one, which is not a majority of two.

variants.title: Choose the read
variants.context: A linearizable read returns state current in the global order but needs a live consensus path. A serializable read is served from one member’s local applied state and may be stale. Watch streams are ordered by revision but are not linearizable reads. A learner replicates without voting.
variants.prompt: A scheduler must never act on stale ownership data. Which read?
optionFeedback: Linearizable reads return state current in the global order.
Serializable reads can be stale.
Watches are ordered but not linearizable.
variants.explanation: Linearizable reads depend on a live consensus path; that is the price of freshness.

variants.title: Choose the read
variants.context: A linearizable read returns state current in the global order but needs a live consensus path. A serializable read is served from one member’s local applied state and may be stale. Watch streams are ordered by revision but are not linearizable reads. A learner replicates without voting.
variants.prompt: During a partition an isolated member can still answer a configuration read. Which kind of read is that, and what is its risk?
options: A serializable read from local applied state; it may be stale.
optionFeedback: Local reads stay available but can lag.
Linearizable reads need quorum.
Transactions need the leader and a majority.
variants.hint: Which read does not need the leader?
variants.explanation: Serializable reads trade freshness for availability.

variants.title: Choose the read
variants.context: A linearizable read returns state current in the global order but needs a live consensus path. A serializable read is served from one member’s local applied state and may be stale. Watch streams are ordered by revision but are not linearizable reads. A learner replicates without voting.
variants.prompt: Adding a learner member: does failure tolerance increase?
options: No. A learner replicates without voting until promoted.
Yes, if it is caught up.
optionFeedback: Learners reduce the risk of adding an uninitialized voter.
Only voters count toward quorum.
Being caught up does not make it a voter.
variants.explanation: Promote a learner only after it has caught up.

variants.title: Build list-and-watch
variants.context: Build a list-and-watch client: read a complete prefix and record its header revision; install the snapshot atomically; watch from the next revision, apply events in order; relist after compaction.
variants.prompt: A controller caches a keyspace prefix. Put the client steps in order.

items.text: Read the complete prefix with the required consistency and record the response header revision.
Replace the local snapshot atomically so readers never see a half-built cache.
Watch from the next revision, apply events in order, and deduplicate reconnects.
If the start revision is compacted, discard the cache, read a new snapshot, and re-establish the watch.

variants.hint: The snapshot revision is the watch boundary.
variants.explanation: List → install → watch → relist after compaction.

variants.title: Build list-and-watch
variants.context: Build a list-and-watch client: read a complete prefix and record its header revision; install the snapshot atomically; watch from the next revision, apply events in order; relist after compaction.
variants.prompt: A watch reconnects after a network blip. Put the steps in order.

items.text: The cache holds the revision of the last applied event.
Reconnect the watch from that revision plus one.
Apply events in order and deduplicate any overlap.
If etcd reports the revision was compacted, relist from a fresh snapshot.

variants.hint: Reconnect from the last processed revision, not from now.
variants.explanation: Compaction is why relist must be part of the design.

variants.title: Build list-and-watch
variants.context: Build a list-and-watch client: read a complete prefix and record its header revision; install the snapshot atomically; watch from the next revision, apply events in order; relist after compaction.
variants.prompt: Freshness matters for a routing table. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Take a linearizable snapshot of the prefix and record its revision.
Watch after that revision and monitor watch progress against a current read.
Relist when the watch falls behind compaction.

variants.explanation: Reconcile the watch with an explicit list-and-watch revision boundary.

variants.title: Design the lock
variants.context: A lease answers whether etcd still receives keep-alives; it does not stop an old process from writing elsewhere after a pause. Acquire ownership with a transaction on key absence or revision, treat the revision as a fencing token, stop work when keep-alive is uncertain, and make external actions idempotent.
variants.prompt: A worker holds a leased lock, pauses for garbage collection past the TTL, then writes to the database. What stops the stale write?
options: A fencing token from the ownership key’s revision that the database validates.
optionFeedback: The destination must participate with fencing or idempotency.
A lease cannot stop an external write.
Shorter TTLs make pauses more likely to break it.

variants.title: Design the lock
variants.context: A lease answers whether etcd still receives keep-alives; it does not stop an old process from writing elsewhere after a pause. Acquire ownership with a transaction on key absence or revision, treat the revision as a fencing token, stop work when keep-alive is uncertain, and make external actions idempotent.
variants.prompt: How should a process acquire exclusive ownership?
options: A transaction that creates the key only if it does not exist or still has the expected revision.
A put with a random value.
A read followed by a put.
optionFeedback: Compare-then-mutate is atomic in one revision.
A blind put overwrites another owner.
Read-then-put races.
variants.explanation: Use a transaction with a version, revision, or lease comparison.

variants.title: Design the lock
variants.context: A lease answers whether etcd still receives keep-alives; it does not stop an old process from writing elsewhere after a pause. Acquire ownership with a transaction on key absence or revision, treat the revision as a fencing token, stop work when keep-alive is uncertain, and make external actions idempotent.
variants.prompt: Keep-alive responses stop arriving. What should the owner do?
options: Stop work now; do not wait until a best guess about TTL expiry.
optionFeedback: Uncertain keep-alive means uncertain ownership.
Another owner may already exist.
TTLs are server-managed.
variants.hint: What does uncertainty about the lease mean for ownership?
variants.explanation: Stop when keep-alive or watch progress is uncertain.

variants.title: Keep etcd in scope
variants.context: etcd is for small coordination state, not blobs, analytics, queues, or caches. Endpoint reachability is not quorum. Revisions are safer coordination inputs than wall-clock timestamps.
variants.prompt: A team wants to store session blobs and run analytics queries in etcd. Is that a fit?
options: No. Keep values and keyspaces small; use systems designed for those workloads.
optionFeedback: etcd is for small coordination state.
It is not a general document or blob store.
Members add coordination cost, not data capacity.
variants.explanation: Configuration, registration, election, ownership: small and important.

variants.title: Keep etcd in scope
variants.context: etcd is for small coordination state, not blobs, analytics, queues, or caches. Endpoint reachability is not quorum. Revisions are safer coordination inputs than wall-clock timestamps.
variants.prompt: A client can reach an endpoint. Does that mean the cluster has quorum?
options: No. Endpoint reachability is not quorum; writes still need a voting majority.
Yes, if the endpoint is the leader.
optionFeedback: Clients should know multiple endpoints and expect unavailability without quorum.
Reachability is a client-side fact.
Leadership does not create a majority.
variants.explanation: Client endpoints, peer consensus, and storage are separate boundaries.

variants.title: Keep etcd in scope
variants.context: etcd is for small coordination state, not blobs, analytics, queues, or caches. Endpoint reachability is not quorum. Revisions are safer coordination inputs than wall-clock timestamps.
variants.prompt: Two services compare wall-clock timestamps to decide who owns a shard. What is safer?
options: Use etcd revisions: create and modification revisions are safer coordination inputs than clocks.
optionFeedback: Revisions advance in one durable order.
Clocks on different machines drift.
Randomness is not order.
variants.hint: Which value advances in a single order?
variants.explanation: Every mutation advances the cluster-wide MVCC revision.
